proof:
# Finite lattice-free facet certificates for a nonempty depth region

Let n>=1,d>=0, let C be a convex body, and let mu be a probability measure supported on S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d). Fix 0<alpha<1. Define

D_alpha={y: every closed ambient halfspace H containing y has mu(H)>=alpha}.

Assume D_alpha is nonempty and D_alpha intersect Lambda is empty. The nonemptiness assumption is explicit; it does not follow merely from the conjectural value of alpha.

## 1. A closed-halfspace representation

D_alpha is precisely the intersection of all closed halfspaces K with mu(K)>1-alpha.

If y has depth at least alpha and is outside such a K, a closed halfspace through y lying in K's open complement has mass below alpha, a contradiction. Conversely, if a bad closed H containing y has mass below alpha, its open complement has mass above1-alpha. An increasing sequence of closed halfspaces strictly inside that complement has the same limiting mass, so one has mass above1-alpha and excludes y. This proves the representation, including boundary mass.

It follows that D_alpha is closed and convex. It lies in C, because a point outside compact convex C can be separated from it by a closed halfspace of mass zero. Thus D_alpha is compact.

## 2. Finite full-dimensional polyhedral approximation with lattice exclusion

Because S is compact and disjoint from D_alpha, finitely many large-mass closed halfspaces K_1,...,K_N satisfy

S intersect K_1 intersect ... intersect K_N=empty.

Indeed their open complements cover S, and compactness gives a finite subcover. Write K_i={w:u_i dot w<=c_i}. Expand each by replacing c_i with c_i+1/j. Also choose outer polytopes C_j such that C is contained in int(C_j), the C_j lie in a fixed bounded set, and their Hausdorff distance to C tends to zero. One explicit construction takes all grid cubes of side1/j that meet C, forms the convex hull of their vertices, and then adds the cube[-1/j,1/j]^{n+d}. This polytope contains C in its interior and lies within Euclidean distance2sqrt(n+d)/j of C.

Put

Q_j=C_j intersect intersection_i {w:u_i dot w<=c_i+1/j}.

Every Q_j has nonempty interior: any fixed point of D_alpha is strictly inside all the expanded inequalities and C_j. For all sufficiently large j, Q_j avoids Lambda. Otherwise a bounded sequence y_j in Q_j intersect Lambda has a convergent subsequence; its integer coordinates eventually stabilize, and the limit lies in C intersect Lambda intersect all K_i, a contradiction.

Choose such a Q=Q_j. It is a full-dimensional compact polytope containing D_alpha and avoiding Lambda. Write all its defining inequalities as

a_i dot z+beta_i dot x<=c_i, i=1,...,m.

Every excluded open cap H_i={a_i dot z+beta_i dot x>c_i} has mu(H_i)<alpha. For expanded K_i this follows from their original large mass; for the outer-polytope inequalities the excluded cap has mass zero.

## 3. Exact elimination and minimal positive dependences

The projection P=pi(Q) is a full-dimensional compact polytope avoiding Z^n. By Farkas' lemma, z belongs to P precisely when

(sum_i lambda_i a_i) dot z <= sum_i lambda_i c_i

for every lambda>=0 satisfying sum_i lambda_i beta_i=0.

The nonnegative kernel cone is generated by its minimal-support nonzero vectors. Such a vector has at most d+1 positive coordinates. To verify the support bound, if its support J had size>d+1, the kernel of the d by |J| matrix of beta columns would have dimension at least two. A kernel vector independent of lambda permits a nontrivial perturbation that keeps all coordinates nonnegative and drives one to zero, leaving a nonzero kernel vector with smaller support, a contradiction. The same argument shows uniqueness up to scaling on a minimal support. There are finitely many supports. Subtracting suitably scaled minimal-support vectors, each time removing a positive coordinate, decomposes any nonnegative kernel vector into these generators.

Thus P has a finite halfspace description using inequalities generated by at most d+1 original inequalities each. Every actual facet of the full-dimensional P coincides with one of these describing hyperplanes: at a relative interior point of a facet, at least one of the finite defining inequalities is active, and its hyperplane must contain the facet.

Accordingly, for each facet j there is a positive multiplier vector on an index set I_j, |I_j|<=d+1, with

sum_{i in I_j} lambda_{ji} beta_i=0,
ell_j=sum_{i in I_j} lambda_{ji} a_i !=0,
delta_j=sum_{i in I_j} lambda_{ji} c_i,

and facet inequality ell_j dot z<=delta_j.

At any lifted contact point (z_j,x_j) in Q with ell_j dot z_j=delta_j, every inequality in I_j is active:

a_i dot z_j+beta_i dot x_j=c_i for i in I_j.

Indeed their nonnegative slacks have a positive weighted sum equal to zero, so each slack vanishes. These are the exact contact and balance equations.

## 4. At most2^n facets, and the resulting numerical constant

Apply Doignon's theorem to the finite family of facet halfspaces of P. Since their intersection avoids Z^n, some r<=2^n of them already define a polyhedron L avoiding Z^n. L contains P, and each selected facet hyperplane touches P. L need not be bounded or maximal lattice-free; neither property is needed.

For each selected facet define its exterior mixed cap

E_j=S intersect { (z,x):ell_j dot z>delta_j }.

The E_j cover S, because no integer projection belongs to L. If a point belongs to E_j, then

sum_{i in I_j} lambda_{ji}(a_i dot z+beta_i dot x-c_i)>0,

so at least one original open bad cap H_i contains it. Therefore

mu(E_j)<=sum_{i in I_j}mu(H_i)<|I_j|alpha<=(d+1)alpha.

Summing over the cover gives

1<=sum_{j=1}^r mu(E_j)<r(d+1)alpha<=2^n(d+1)alpha.

This recovers precisely the Helly-number threshold1/[2^n(d+1)]. The derivation is exact and handles oblique original cuts, vertical facets, zero-mass support constraints, and closed-boundary mass.

## What has not been proved

The contact point z_j is a real projection point, not generally an integer point. The multiplier balance gives a union covering inequality, not a conditional log-concave measure on E_j and not a gamma_d bound for that cap. The above equations alone do not replace d+1 by1/gamma_d.

No maximizer of a volume or determinant potential has been assumed to exist. No stationarity or allocation identities beyond the explicitly proved finite Farkas contact equations have been asserted. The case D_alpha=empty remains outside this facet construction and needs a separate argument.
